globals.note: Illustrative model. Hormuz uses IEA 2025 figures (Kpler ship-tracking); other chokepoints use 1H 2025 tanker-tracking flows (Vortexa data, published by EIA). Flows passing more than one chokepoint are counted at each, so combined totals are an upper bound.

sources.name: EIA — Today in Energy: Strait of Hormuz

bypass.note: Saudi Abqaiq→Yanbu, 7 mb/d since the 2026 NGL-to-crude conversion (Aramco; 5 mb/d in 2018). ~2 mb/d was in use in early 2026, leaving 3–5 mb/d spare depending on Red Sea export capacity (IEA). Low end counted.
UAE Habshan→Fujairah (ADCOP), ~1.8 mb/d; ~1.1 mb/d already used, leaving up to 0.7 mb/d (IEA). Low end counted.
Iraq→Turkey, ~1.6 mb/d nameplate. Restarted 18 Mar 2026 at ~250 kb/d; usable volume depends on Baghdad–Erbil–Ankara politics. Not counted.

strait-of-hormuz.bypass_note: IEA estimates 3.5–5.5 mb/d of Saudi and UAE pipeline capacity could bypass Hormuz; the model counts the low end. Iran's Goreh–Jask line is effectively non-operational. Iraq's Basra, Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain exports and all Qatari/UAE LNG (just over 112 bcm, almost 20% of global LNG trade) have no bypass. Most of the world's spare crude capacity (>4 mb/d, mainly Saudi) also sits behind the strait.

exposed.note: 4.6 mb/d of Hormuz crude in 2025, the largest single destination (IEA/Kpler).
2.1 mb/d of Hormuz crude; with Bangladesh and Pakistan, received almost two-thirds of its LNG via Hormuz.
Part of 6.2 mb/d of crude to 'other Asia'; IEA calls both particularly reliant on Hormuz flows.
Gas is 50% and 25% of their power mix; LNG shortfalls hit electricity supply directly.
Only ~0.6 mb/d of crude and ~7% of its LNG came via Hormuz, but exposed through global prices.

sources.name: IEA — Strait of Hormuz Factsheet (Feb 2026, based on Kpler)

bab-el-mandeb.bypass_note: 1H 2025 flows (EIA), already reduced by Houthi attacks; ~8.7 mb/d moved through before them (1H 2023). No pipeline bypass: traffic reroutes around the Cape of Good Hope. Yanbu cargoes heading north to Europe can still reach Suez/SUMED without crossing the strait.

exposed.note: Middle East crude, diesel and jet fuel via Suez; longer voyages raise delivered costs.
Suez Canal and SUMED revenues collapse when traffic diverts.
Yanbu exports (the Hormuz bypass outlet) sit inside the Red Sea.

bypass.note: Ain Sukhna→Sidi Kerir, ~2.5 mb/d capacity. Only helps if tankers can still reach the Red Sea side.

suez-canal.bypass_note: Baseline is Suez Canal + SUMED combined flow, 1H 2023. Baseline: EIA 1H 2025 flows.

exposed.note: Main route for Gulf and Asian oil products and LNG into the Mediterranean and NW Europe.
Canal fees are one of the state's largest sources of foreign currency.

turkish-straits.bypass_note: The Black Sea has no other exit. BTC (Azerbaijan→Ceyhan) is unaffected because it loads on the Mediterranean. Baseline: EIA 1H 2025 flows.

exposed.note: CPC carries ~80% of Kazakh crude exports to Novorossiysk.
Black Sea crude and product exports.
Italy, Greece, Spain and Turkey rely on CPC Blend and Black Sea barrels.

strait-of-malacca.bypass_note: Ships can divert via the Lombok/Makassar or Sunda straits at the cost of ~2–3 extra days. China's overland pipelines (Central Asia, Russia, Myanmar) cover only a small share of its imports. Baseline: EIA 1H 2025 flows.

exposed.note: ~80% of oil imports ("Malacca Dilemma").
Nearly all Gulf crude and LNG passes Malacca or nearby straits.
Same exposure as Japan.
Almost entirely dependent on seaborne energy imports.

panama-canal.bypass_note: US Gulf LNG to Asia diverts via the Cape of Good Hope or Cape Horn, adding ~2 weeks. That ties up LNG carrier capacity and raises Asian spot prices. Oil figure is approximate. Baseline: EIA 1H 2025 flows.

exposed.note: US LNG and LPG cargoes to Northeast Asia.
Longer voyages make Asian sales less competitive; more cargoes default to Europe.
Refined product imports from the US Gulf Coast.
